findings.quote: --task-text "<the task's title and description>"
findings.problem: Five bundled skill files, with byte-identical managed copies under .metaproject/skills/gdskills, tell the executing agent to substitute the task title and description into a double-quoted shell argument of `keryx skills resolve-context`. Inside double quotes a POSIX shell still expands $(...), backticks and $VAR. Markdown task descriptions use backticks all the time. The CLI has no way to read the text from a file or stdin, so the argv string is the only route, and the instruction never says to escape it. The docs example also uses double quotes.
findings.impact: Trigger: a task or issue description contains `cmd` or $(cmd), either by accident (inline code is ubiquitous) or planted by whoever authors the issue. An orchestrator or implementer that follows the template literally runs that command with its own shell permissions before keryx starts. Outcome: arbitrary command execution on the developer's machine or CI, or at minimum a mangled task text that silently stops keyword promotion. The MCP and agent-tool route (`task_text` field) does not go through a shell and is not affected.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the command a shell-safe input path and name it in the skills: a `--task-text-file <path>` (or `--task-text -` for stdin) option, with the instruction to write the description to a file with a quoted heredoc first. Failing that, change the templates to say the text must be single-quoted with embedded single quotes escaped, or passed as `--task-text=$'...'`, and state in the skill that the description is untrusted. Update the bundled and managed copies together (skill-sync.test.ts already checks they are byte-identical).
findings.evidence: flow-orchestrator/SKILL.md line 323 reads: `run keryx skills resolve-context --for test|implement --files ... --task-text "<the task's title and description>" --out ...`. job-orchestrator/orchestrator-prompt.md:132 and :188 and job-orchestrator/SKILL.md:749 and :1307 use `--task-text "<task title and description>"` and `--task-text "<fix task description>"`. task-implementer/SKILL.md:182 and tests-creator/SKILL.md:93 give the same form, and docs/docs/guides/apply-project-rules.md:170 shows it. resolve-context-command.ts reads the text only through optionValue(args, "--task-text"), with no file or stdin option.

findings.problem: recordLastResolve now writes up to 4000 characters of the raw --task-text into .metaproject/data/skills/project-context/last.json. The path is not in .gitignore (only .metaproject/data/skills/stocktake/ is) and not in renderMetaprojectGitignoreBlock(), and writeContained is called without a mode, so the file is created 0664 (the worktree's own copy is 664). `git check-ignore -v` exits 1 for it, `git status` lists .metaproject/data/skills/ as untracked, and the file here already holds a taskText entry. findings.impact: Trigger: an orchestrator or operator runs `keryx skills resolve-context --task-text "<issue title and body>"`, as the five orchestration skills now instruct for every dispatch. Issue and task bodies routinely hold pasted tokens, connection strings, customer data and logs. Outcome: the text lands in an untracked, non-ignored, group-readable file. A later `git add -A`, `git add .metaproject` or `git add .` commits it and a push publishes it; the repo already tracks hundreds of files under .metaproject/data/review*, so broad adds there are routine. findings.quote: return new RegExp(`(?<![\\p{L}\\p{N}_])${escapeRegExp(keyword)}(?![\\p{L}\\p{N}_])`, "iu").test(text);
findings.problem: The not-a-word-character lookarounds are applied unconditionally. When the keyword itself begins (or ends) with a non-word character, the lookaround demands that the neighbouring text character is also a non-word character, which is the opposite of a word boundary at that edge. Verified at head: keywordOccurs('fix styles.css please', '.css') returns false, keywordOccurs('a@apply', '@apply') returns false, while keywordOccurs('use @apply here', '@apply') returns true.
findings.impact: Trigger: a declaration with a keyword such as '.css', '.scss', '@apply' or '::part' (the natural spelling for a styling document) and a task text like 'fix styles.css' or 'tidy a.scss'. The reference is not promoted and stays on_demand, so the obligation to read STYLING.md is silently skipped. `check` does not warn (a 4-character keyword passes MIN_KEYWORD_CHARACTERS). AC5 says 'on a word boundary', which a conventional \b would satisfy for 'styles.css'.
findings.suggested_fix: Apply each lookaround only when the keyword's edge character is a word character: prefix `(?<![\p{L}\p{N}_])` only if the keyword starts with [\p{L}\p{N}_], suffix `(?![\p{L}\p{N}_])` only if it ends with one. Add a test for '.css' in 'styles.css'.
findings.evidence: Ran keywordOccurs from src/gdskills/reference-entries.ts under bun at head: ('fix styles.css please', '.css') -> false; ('use @apply here', '@apply') -> true; ('a@apply', '@apply') -> false. The regex source is the quoted line.

findings.problem: The resolver and the validator disagree about a declaration whose anchor no longer matches a heading. reference-entries.ts falls back to the whole file and states the obligation: "the whole file (${bytes} bytes) is the obligation" (AC6: fall back with a warning, never silence). The proof module's currentSection returns { ok: false } for the same declaration, wordsFailure turns that into a summary-words failure, and nothing in the worker's control (citing the right anchor, reading the whole file, writing a good summary) can clear it.
findings.impact: Trigger: references.json declares an anchor that is renamed or removed in the document, and a task matches the declaration's condition. Outcome: the resolver tells the worker to read the whole file; the worker does, cites path, sha256, the declared anchor and a real summary; checkResolvedContext still emits a 'summary that cannot be checked' miss on every run. Under enforcement block this makes `flow task done` and the standalone check exit 1 until someone edits references.json, a fix the worker was never told about by the validator line. The fallback the resolver advertises is not honoured by the checker that enforces it.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the proof the same fallback the resolver uses: in currentSection, when extractSection returns found: false, return { ok: true, text, what: "the file" } (the whole file, matching the resolver's stated obligation) and keep the anchor-not-found problem in `references check` and the resolve warning. If fail-closed is intended instead, make the resolver demote or refuse the entry with the same wording rather than promising a whole-file obligation, and say so in the validator line.
findings.evidence: Diff, reference-entries.ts resolveReferences: when !section.found it sets sectionBytes = bytes and pushes a warning ending 'the whole file (...) is the obligation', and the entry stays must_read. Diff, reference-proof.ts currentSection: `if (!section.found) return { ok: false, why: ... }`; wordsFailure: `if (!section.ok) return { rule: "summary-words", detail: ... cannot be checked ... }`; proofFailures always calls wordsFailure when a summary exists. The only inputs are entry.anchor (from the resolver output) and the file text, so no worker-supplied value can make currentSection succeed.

findings.quote: A linked rule (registered in place, not copied) is not scanned.
findings.problem: scanCitations iterates listRuleRefs(), which lists only files copied under .metaproject/rules/project/. The resolver's collectProjectRules also reads rules registered with mode link from their origin and scans their citations. The authoring checker therefore sees a different rule set from the engine it is authoring for. The header comment records the limit but gives no reason for it, and the limit hits the primary import mode: `keryx skills import --rules <dir> --link` registers rules in place and copies nothing.
findings.impact: Trigger: a project whose rules are linked (import --rules --link) and which cite STYLING.md or similar. Outcomes: (1) undeclaredCitationHint finds nothing, so the AC15 closing lines (undeclared count and the command to run) never print after a --link import; (2) `references suggest` omits the documents cited only by linked rules; (3) `references check` reports 'unused-declaration: no project rule cites this document' for a declaration that a linked rule does cite and the resolver treats as cited. Check output and resolver output disagree about the same project.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the citation set from the same rule source the resolver uses: factor collectProjectRules (or a smaller 'rule texts of this project, copied and linked' function) out of context-resolver.ts and have scanCitations read it, reporting an unreadable or changed link as rule-unreadable. If linked rules are deliberately excluded, state the reason in the header and make the unused-declaration and hint wording say 'copied rules'.
findings.evidence: Diff, references-check.ts scanCitations: `for (const ref of (await listRuleRefs(projectRoot)).sort(compare))`. Head src/gdskills/context-resolver.ts: listRuleRefs is `return listRuleFiles(projectRoot)` (copied files only), while collectProjectRules adds `registry.keys()` and reads `resolveOriginPath(entry.origin, projectRoot)` for entries with mode link. Diff, import-rules.ts: the hint is computed by undeclaredCitationHint(process.cwd()) with no regard to --link.

findings.problem: scanHeadings matches every line with a lazy `(.*?)` followed by `[ \t]*$`, and stripClosingHashes then runs `/[ \t]+#+$/` over the captured text. Both backtrack quadratically on a heading line that holds a long run of spaces or tabs followed by a non-space character. scanHeadings runs on the whole declared document whenever an anchor is resolved, checked or proven, and the size cap is 262144 bytes (CONTRACT_MAX_BYTES), so the line can be that long.
findings.impact: Trigger: a contributor changes a markdown document that references.json declares with an anchor (STYLING.md style), adding one heading line such as `## x` + 120000 spaces + `x`. The next `keryx skills resolve-context`, `keryx skills references check`, `keryx skills contracts validate --resolved`, or a TUI status refresh (loadProjectContextStatus -> checkReferences) runs extractSection synchronously. Measured on this head with bun: 20000 spaces = 0.37 s, 60000 = 3.3 s, 120000 = 13.2 s, and the cost grows with the square, so a 250 KB line is about a minute of 100% CPU with the event loop blocked. A reviewer who checks out a hostile PR hangs the CLI and freezes the TUI. A file with no anchor in its declaration is not scanned.
findings.suggested_fix: Make heading detection linear. Match `^ {0,3}(#{1,6})(?:[ \t]+(.*))?$` (no trailing-whitespace group), then `trimEnd()` in code. Replace the closing-hash strip with a linear step: after trimEnd, take the trailing `#` run and drop it only if the character before it is a space or tab, and treat a text made only of hashes as empty. Optionally skip lines longer than a few thousand characters as non-headings.

findings.quote: body.add(new Ctor(renderer, { id: `projectctx-${tab}`, content: stylePlanText(otui, lines.join("\n"), "plain") }));
findings.problem: paint() joins the lines built by formatProjectReferencesLines and passes them to a TextRenderable as is; stylePlanText with tone "plain" returns the string untouched. The new References tab puts attacker-writable strings into those lines with no escaping: declaration.path, declaration.anchor, every glob and keyword (conditionText), declaration.description (shown in the "on demand" row), the invalid-file messages (label() interpolates the raw path and the JSON.parse reason), and the finding messages (anchor-not-found lists up to 12 heading texts read from the declared document, unused-declaration and the others quote the path). All of them come from .metaproject/rules/project/references.json or from the documents it names, which are committed project files. JSON allows \u001b and \r in any of these strings, and parseReferences only trims them. The repository's own rule for exactly this input (src/lib/terminal-safe.ts: hooks.json is 'a committed file an attacker fully controls'; research-sync-panel.ts: 'The page is a file in the working tree: ... escaped before it reaches the terminal'; external-diff-modal.ts) is to pass such strings through terminalSafe/terminalSafeBlock. This modal and the new tab skip it.
findings.impact: Trigger: a user clones or checks out a repository whose references.json (or a declared .md heading) carries an escape sequence, for example description "x\u001b[1A\u001b[2K..." or a heading with the same, and runs /projectctx refs (or opens the References tab). Observed in a probe: createTestRenderer with a TextRenderable holding "AB\u001b[2JCD\u001b[1A..." keeps the ESC bytes in the cell buffer (captureCharFrame returns them verbatim) and a bare \r starts a new row, so the sequences reach the cell contents that the renderer writes out; I did not capture the final byte stream sent to a real terminal. Outcome if they are emitted: cursor movement or line erase can repaint rows of the modal, for instance to hide a problems (n) line or to forge 'promoted' / 'matched glob' rows, in a view the operator reads to decide whether the rules are being applied. Bidi and zero-width characters also pass, so a path can read differently from what it is. The ordinary sidebar line is not affected (see clean areas).
findings.suggested_fix: Escape in the one sink, paint(): content: stylePlanText(otui, terminalSafeBlock(lines.join("\n")).text, "plain") with import { terminalSafeBlock } from "../lib/terminal-safe". terminalSafeBlock keeps \n and \t and replaces ESC, \r, U+2028/2029, bidi and zero-width code points with visible \xHH / \uHHHH, so line counts (and the contentRows computation) are unchanged and all three tabs are covered, including the pre-existing Last resolve tab. Add a test in project-context-inspector.test.ts: a references.json whose description, anchor, glob and keyword contain \u001b[2K and \r must not put an ESC or CR in the renderable's content.

findings.problem: The operator runbook tells the person running the live run that the summary must share at least two distinct words of five or more letters with the section, and treats a failure as a sign that the two-word threshold is too strict. findings.problem: The `declaration()` fixture builder nests a ternary inside a ternary inside an object spread to express 'a key present in overrides with value undefined removes the field'. It is the hardest line to read in a 329-line file, and every test in the file goes through it.
findings.impact: A reader changing a fixture (adding a field, or another optional one like `anchor`) has to decode the double ternary and its `in` test first; the next optional field would copy the same pattern.
findings.suggested_fix: Merge then delete: `const merged = { ...entry, ...overrides }; if (merged.anchor === undefined) delete merged.anchor; return merged as Declaration;` (the `Overrides` type already admits `undefined`), or an early-return `if` for the anchor case.
findings.evidence: src/commands/skills-references.test.ts, function `declaration`: the `"anchor" in overrides ? (... ? {} : {...}) : {...}` expression inside the returned object literal.

In the test the citations enter the Map in rule-text order (STYLING.md, then THEMING.md), which already equals the sorted order, so deleting `.sort(compare)` in undeclaredCitations (references-check.ts:145) leaves the assertion green. Only one rule file exists in any test, so `.sort(compare)` over rule refs (line 96), the `!by.includes(rulePath)` de-duplication (line 109) and the 'cited by <rules>' message of undeclared-citation (line 225) are never exercised; the undeclared-citation test asserts only `code:path`, never the message.
findings.impact: Sorted output is a stated property of suggest ('Sorted by path' in the doc comment) and makes the printed skeleton and the check report stable across file systems. A later edit to the scan can reorder output or double-list a rule that cites one document twice with the suite green.

Assert the path order, and in the check test assert that the undeclared-citation message names each citing rule once.

findings.quote: await project({ references: [declaration({ description: "Styling rules." })] });
findings.problem: The three numeric thresholds are pinned only far from the boundary. The description fixture is 14 characters against a limit of 20 (references-check.ts:188, `< MIN_DESCRIPTION_CHARACTERS`), the keywords are 3 and 2 characters against 4 (line 192), and the oversize document is 262145 'x' plus a heading against CONTRACT_MAX_BYTES 262144 (line 133, `>`). Changing `<` to `<=` or `>` to `>=` in any of the three, or moving a limit by a few units, keeps the suite green. No fixture has a 19/20-character description, a 3/4-character keyword, or a document of exactly 262144 bytes.
findings.impact: AC14 states the limits as numbers ('under 20 characters', 'under 4 characters'); an off-by-one edit changes which declarations warn without any test noticing. The cost is to the next editor of these constants.
findings.suggested_fix: Add boundary rows: a description of exactly 20 characters and one of 19, a keyword of exactly 4 and one of 3 (expect no warning, one warning), and a document of exactly CONTRACT_MAX_BYTES bytes (no error) beside the existing one-over case.
findings.evidence: Read the fixtures in the description-short, keyword-short and document-too-large tests against the guards at references-check.ts:133, 188, 192. Reasoned, not run. mutant candidates m5, m6, m7 below.

findings.problem: The test is named 'lists only citations that name a file inside the project' but no cited path in it is outside the project AND exists. `../outside.md` is never created beside the temp root, so it is excluded by inspectDocument returning 'missing', exactly as `docs/missing.md` is; it does not exercise the escaping-path rejection in normaliseCitedPath (references-config.ts) that the name claims. `core/other.mdc` is never captured at all, because DOCUMENT_CITATION (references-check.ts:82) only matches a backticked `.md`. Deleting the escape rejection in normaliseCitedPath therefore leaves this test green (the other test that creates a symlink out of the root covers the declared path via isPathInside, not a cited, undeclared one).
findings.impact: The next author reads the test as coverage of the 'inside the project' filter for undeclared citations. A cited `../SECRET.md` that exists would be offered by suggest if the normaliser guard regressed, with this suite green. May already be pinned by references-config.test.ts, which is outside this slice.
findings.suggested_fix: Create `outside.md` in the parent of the temp root (or a sibling temp dir reached through `../`) before running suggest, so the only thing excluding it is the path guard; keep `docs/missing.md` as the separate 'does not exist' case.
findings.evidence: Read the fixture (files: STYLING.md, THEMING.md only), references-check.ts:82,106 and inspectDocument. I did not open references-config.ts's tests (other slice), hence the lowered confidence.

findings.quote: [--task-type <type>] [--max-bytes <n>] [--out <path>] [--json]
findings.problem: The diff edits printResolveContextHelp to add `--task-text`, and docs/docs/cli-reference.md (line 3452) shows `[--task-type <type>] [--task-text <text>] [--max-bytes <n>] [--out <path>] [--json]`, but the usage block of printSkillsHelp (`keryx skills --help`), two lines above the new `keryx skills references` lines the diff adds, still omits `--task-text`. findings.quote: --task-text "<the task's title and description>"
findings.problem: Flow 462 makes every resolve-context dispatch in flow-orchestrator, job-orchestrator, task-implementer and tests-creator pass the task title and description as one double-quoted shell argument. That text comes from issue bodies and plans. In double quotes the shell still expands `$(...)`, backticks and `$VAR`, a literal `"` ends the argument early, and a description over the kernel's single-argument limit (about 128 KiB on Linux) cannot be passed at all. The resolver cuts the text to 4000 characters only after it has arrived as argv.
findings.impact: Trigger: an issue or plan description that contains a backtick span or `$(...)` (common in issue text that quotes code or commands), or a stray double quote. A dispatching agent that pastes it verbatim has the shell run the embedded command, or gets a syntax error or a truncated --task-text. The truncated case is silent: the keyword match then runs on a cut text and a keyword-promoted reference is not promoted, with no warning. Frequency is low because the dispatcher is a model that may quote by hand; the cost when it does not is a command run from untrusted text.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not tell the dispatcher to inline free text. Either add a `--task-text-file <path>` (or `--task-text -` for stdin) and have the skills write the task description to a file first, or state in the prose that the text is passed single-quoted with embedded single quotes escaped, and name the first ~500 characters as enough (the resolver keeps 4000). The same sentence appears in job-orchestrator/SKILL.md, job-orchestrator/orchestrator-prompt.md, task-implementer/SKILL.md and tests-creator/SKILL.md.
findings.evidence: Slice hunks at flow-orchestrator/SKILL.md (resolve-context line before 'Dispatch payload'), job-orchestrator/SKILL.md Step A and fix loop item 3, orchestrator-prompt.md steps 1 and FIX item 2, task-implementer/SKILL.md 2.0c, tests-creator/SKILL.md 1.2b. runResolveContextCommand reads the flag with optionValue(args, "--task-text") and truncates later in truncateTaskText (context-resolver.ts), so no input path avoids argv.
